title: The Man with the Golden Arm
summary: Josh and Chuck profile James Harrison, the Australian blood and plasma donor known as "the Man with the Golden Arm," whose antibodies were used to make anti-D immunoglobulin that prevents Rh disease in newborns. The episode explains Rh incompatibility and hemolytic disease of the newborn, the 1958 work of John Gorman and the Sing Sing prisoner tests, the Gorman family's Heathrow pickup, Harrison's childhood lung removal and transfusion, his more than 1,100 donations, his death in February 2025, the rare anti-D donors in Australia and elsewhere, and global and US donation rates. The episode also includes ad breaks, casual banter, and a listener correction about the heavy metal episode on Rob Halford and Denim leather.
topics: Stuff You Should Know listener mail

segments.title: Cockroach banter and episode setup
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck trade cockroach stories and introduce the episode about James Harrison.

segments.title: Rh factor and Rh incompatibility
segments.summary: Explanation of the Rh factor on red blood cells, how Rh-negative mothers can form antibodies against Rh-positive babies, and why a first pregnancy is usually fine while later ones are at risk.

segments.title: Discovery of Rh factor and early anti-D idea
segments.summary: The Rh factor was identified in 1939 after a stillbirth and transfusion reaction; in 1958 John Gorman proposed giving Rh-negative mothers Rh antibodies to prevent their own antibody production.

segments.title: Sing Sing trials and Gorman family treatment
segments.summary: Gorman's team tested the anti-D injection on male prisoners at Sing Sing, then gave it to his sister-in-law Kath, who was Rh-negative, at Heathrow pickup as she went into labor; she then had healthy sons.

segments.title: James Harrison's early life and calling
segments.summary: At age fourteen Harrison had a lung removed and received about two gallons of blood in transfusions, which inspired him to become a donor; he was a clerk and his wife Barbara was a teacher, and he donated plasma frequently on vacations.

segments.title: Plasma versus whole blood donation
segments.summary: Comparison of plasma and whole blood donation time and process, and how often Harrison donated, including his employer's reaction.

segments.title: Harrison's family and fear of needles
segments.summary: Harrison's daughter and granddaughter-in-law received anti-D treatment; his grandson began donating; he donated after Barbara's death in 2005 despite hating needles, and mostly used his right arm.

segments.title: Harrison's retirement and humility
segments.summary: Harrison kept donating until 2018 when he was 81 and was told to stop; he was modest, and he received the Medal of the Order of Australia in 1999.
topics: Medal of the Order of Australia

segments.title: Harrison quotes and Jason T-shirt banter
segments.summary: Quotes from Harrison about his talent for donating, followed by banter about a 'What would Jason do' shirt.

segments.title: Harrison's death and rare anti-D donors
segments.summary: Harrison died in February 2025 at 88; he was one of few people whose blood makes anti-D; the Rh Ladies of Winnipeg donated plasma in Canada, including Mary Tell.

segments.title: Australian anti-D donors and sensitization
segments.summary: Fewer than two hundred anti-D donors in Australia; Kieran Freese, a midwife, was sensitized to produce antibodies and had to send hysterectomy records to Lifeblood; a matched anonymous donor gives blood for her.

segments.title: Global and US blood donation rates
segments.summary: Half of women needing treatment worldwide don't get it; the US has 3 percent donation rate versus Australia's 14 percent, with comparisons to the UK, France, and other countries.

segments.title: Listener mail: heavy metal correction
segments.summary: Listener Joshua Ernsberger corrects the heavy metal episode, saying Rob Halford's leather style came from bands like Saxon rather than S and M clubs, citing Halford's book.
